title: Beyond Data: Imperfect Physics as a Prior for Reinforcement Learning
detail: Reinforcement learning (RL) promises agents that can improve through experience using only the supervision provided by a reward function. In robotics, however, real-world interaction is expensive, dense rewards are difficult to specify, and sparse rewards often lead to sample-inefficient learning. In this talk, I explore whether imperfect physics priors can nevertheless provide useful structure for RL.  Focusing on goal-conditioned RL (GCRL) for robot navigation and manipulation, I show how control-theoretic principles can serve as inductive biases for policy learning. We first connect goal-reaching value functions to time-to-go fields and interpret the Eikonal equation as a simplified surrogate for the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, motivating Eikonal-informed value learning for challenging navigation problems. We then study its interaction with the quasimetric structure typical of GCRL. Their combination reveals the limitations of imposing these priors globally and motivates a hierarchical formulation. This becomes particularly important in contact-rich manipulation, where hybrid dynamics induce state-dependent controllability and motivate applying physics-informed structure only to appropriate state representations.

title: Revisiting the Effectiveness of LLM Pruning for Test-Time Scaling
detail: Large Language Models (LLMs) now exhibit remarkable growth in reasoning capabilities through test-time scaling (TTS). TTS uses additional compute during inference by generating thinking tokens. While TTS has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, these improvements come at the cost of increased inference time and computational demands. Model pruning provides a promising way to reduce these computational requirements by removing redundant parameters from the model. However, previous work has shown that naively pruning reasoning models can lead to severe degradation in performance. In this talk, I will show that, unlike structured pruning approaches that past work has explored in the context of reasoning and TTS, unstructured pruning methods can retain reasoning performance comparable to the full model, and at times even exceeding it. I will conclude by discussing what these findings reveal about reasoning models and their broader implications for building more efficient AI systems without sacrificing capability.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Designing Responsible AI and Data Science for Social Good
detail:
What should AI systems optimize when they shape people’s opportunities, well-being, and access to essential 
services? This presentation examines that questions through responsible AI, where fairness, 
transparency, privacy, robustness, and social benefit are built into technical objectives rather than treated as 
afterthoughts. Drawing on the INFORMS Journal on Computing special issue, it links advances in machine 
learning and operations research to challenges in justice, education, healthcare, and digital communication. 
Selected studies will show how the meaning of better AI varies by context, from evaluating educational content and 
protecting health data to detecting misinformation and identifying differences across population groups. Examples from 
college admissions and confidence-aware fake-news detection will demonstrate why accuracy alone is insufficient: 
institutional interactions can affect fairness, and even confident predictions may require closer scrutiny. The presentation 
concludes by outlining a research agenda for generative and agentic AI centered on bias propagation, human-AI 
collaboration, lifecycle accountability, and long-term social impact. It calls for AI success to be measured not only by 
predictive performance, but also by how responsibly decision systems serve people.

title: Golden Layers and Where to Find Them: Improved Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models Via Layer Gradient Analysis
detail: Updating a model’s knowledge through training is computationally expensive and risks catastrophic forgetting. Knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) provides an alternative by updating the model’s knowledge for a specific query to a desired target while preserving its behavior on unrelated queries. This process typically involves two stages: identifying the layer to edit and updating its parameters. Intuitively, different query samples may localize knowledge at different layers of the model, suggesting different sample-wise editing performance for a fixed editing layer. However, in our NeurIPS 2026 paper, we hypothesize the existence of fixed golden layers that can achieve near-optimal editing performance similar to sample-wise optimal layers. To validate this hypothesis, we provide empirical evidence by comparing golden layers against ground-truth sample-wise optimal layers. Furthermore, we show that golden layers can be reliably identified using a proxy dataset and generalize effectively to unseen test set queries across datasets. Finally, we propose a novel method, namely Layer Gradient Analysis (LGA), that estimates golden layers efficiently via gradient-attribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our LGA approach across different LLM types and various knowledge editing methods.

title: The Sociotechnical Imagination of Musical Machinery and Ecology: Analyzing the Technological Promises of AI Music Creation
detail:
"The sociotechnical imaginaries of AI produce technological promises subject to a cycle of hype, disillusionment, and criticism. These future prognostications evolve as AI’s capabilities expand, even as they result in a process of routinization, yielding artistic approaches rooted in the technology’s failure to realize these espoused promises. The sociotechnical imaginary is a useful lens to examine how technological promises have produced AI-enhanced music practices from a pragmatism that continually reconciles with a techno-utopian futurity. 
 The persuasiveness of AI’s evolving technological promise has shaped discourses, expectations, and disillusion towards the present and future of musical creation. The myth of the intelligent machine—an assemblage or apparatus that cannot just automate human labor but possesses creative agency—contains philosophical and creative implications for musical intelligence in an age when an AI ecology consolidates the roles involved in music composition and performance while accelerating the process of its production. 
 This talk examines three case studies that traverse the development of the AI’s sociotechnical imaginaries, relating them to music creation. These instruments and platforms—Minsky and Friedkin’s Triadex Muse, Puckett and Zicarelli’s Max/Msp~/Jitter, and the current commercial end-to-end AI-driven music platforms for hyper-reproduction, were developed in response to a contextualized cycle of hype, disillusion, and criticism. The routinization brought upon by the disillusion voiced towards the preceding technological promises greatly informed the creative scope and ambition in the following epoch of sociotechnological imaginaries. 
 These case studies will be used to critique AI-driven music production under the latest era of the sociotechnical imaginary, demonstrating that contemporary technological promises will also be subject to an inevitable process of routinization. Yet, there are opportunities for bridging the previous imaginaries with the present promises, which can foster a routinization process that centers the performer as the real-time interlocutor between an evolving technological assemblage and their own musical intelligence, agency, and creativity.
 Rather than focusing on AI’s rote technical functionality, these case studies and supporting theoretical sources will be used to both critique and confront these existing technological promises, and leverage them into contemplating the future of human-centered technological mediation in music creation. "
speaker: Steven Lewis
bio: Steven Lewis joined the University of South Florida’s Music Faculty in August of 2025, as Assistant Professor of Artificial Intelligence and Entrepreneurism in the Arts. As a percussionist, music technologist and multimedia artist, Steven’s creative practice centers on designing multimodal interactive music systems, augmented instruments, and controllers that leverage emergent technologies in creative domains that emphasize live sound processing and improvisation between the human and the computer. His research focuses on analyzing the ontological, political, and economic transformations that AI has catalyzed in experimental and institutionalized music, with an emphasis on theorizing about on the convergence of virtuosity and creativity in AI-mediated performance and composition. His research and creative work has been accepted at the New York Electronic Music Festival, The Society of Electroacoustic Music in the United States, the International Computer Music Conference, the International Conference on AI and Music Creativity, the International Sound and Music Computing Conference, the International Timbre Conference, and the conference on 21st Century Musical Practices. He is a PhD graduate of the Improvisation, Composition, and Integrated Technology Program at the University of California, Irvine, and holds graduate degrees in Music Technology from NYU and Jazz Studies at the University of Miami’s Frost School of Music. He is a proud alumni of the University of South Florida.

detail: **Tampa QA Meetup × Tampa JUG Present × Tampa Bay Tech & Beer** AI-assisted coding is quickly becoming the primary way applications are built. While it allows developers to create complex applications and features with only a few prompts, ambiguous language and AI hallucinations can introduce bugs, hidden assumptions, and unintended behavior. Simply asking an AI coding agent to “write tests” isn’t enough to guarantee correctness. **[Billy Korando](https://billykorando.com/)** is a Developer Advocate at [Oracle](https://www.oracle.com/) and a member of the Java Platform Group’s Developer Relations team. **What to Expect** Billy will walk through three distinct phases of testing AI-generated code—from defining expected business behavior and covering edge cases to uncovering bugs and risks you may not have anticipated. 🎯 **Highlights** * **Known knowns:** Use specification-driven development to clearly define the expected, business-relevant behavior of your application. * **Known unknowns:** Apply property-based testing to explore edge cases and avoid overfitting and unintended biases. * **Unknown unknowns:** Use static analysis and mutation testing to uncover issues that developers and AI agents may overlook. * **More reliable AI-generated code:** Move beyond simply asking an AI coding agent to “write tests.” * **Stronger test coverage:** Combine complementary testing methods to identify both expected and unexpected failures. * **A reusable testing framework:** Learn an approach that can evolve alongside rapidly changing AI coding tools. **Agenda** **5:45 PM–6:15 PM:** Food and networking **6:15 PM–7:15 PM:** Presentation **7:15 PM–7:45 PM:** Closing and raffle **7:45 PM onward:** Continue the conversation at a nearby bar or restaurant **Location** The event will take place in **DTEC 427.** Please see the attached image for the building and parking locations. **Sponsor** Thank you to our sponsor, **iDelsoft**, for its generous support. **iDelsoft** helps high-growth startups build and scale engineering teams through a network of more than 30,000 vetted developers across 150+ technologies. title: 3D Printing: Models and Slicers (18 Nov 2026)
detail:
This class is offered online. It is open to everyone.

Members should log in for member pricing!

Please note: this is not the tool signoff for 3D printing at Tampa Hackerspace.

This is a hands-on, online class for anyone who is brand new to 3D printing and wants to get up and running with choosing models and getting them ready to print. We recommend that you join this class from a computer you will be using to prepare models for printing, especially if you are a member of Tampa Hackerspace and plan to use the machines at our site. This class does involve installing software on your computer and following along with the instructor; however, there is no final project, and you are free to listen and take notes instead.

We’ll take a look at a few sources for models that you may want to print, and we’ll look at how to tell what kinds of modifications your model might need to print successfully. We’ll walk through setting up PrusaSlicer, an interface that will convert the digital images of your model into toolpaths for the printer to make your model into a physical object. Finally, we’ll take a model from .STL to GCode to show you the full process of getting a print ready for production. Once we’re done, we can cover some questions and answers you may have about 3D printing and, if applicable, joining Tampa Hackerspace.

If you do not already have PrusaSlicer installed, you can download it directly from Prusa (for free!) at https://www.prusa3d.com/en/page/prusaslicer_424/ . We won’t spend much time on the install during class, so you can save yourself some time if you download and install before we meet. I will be in the class a bit early in case you have any questions about downloading and installing the software. (Note that PrusaSlicer runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.)

The member price is for paid members of Tampa Hackerspace. Information on becoming a paid member can be found on our website (http://tampahackerspace.com/membership).
